PROJECT 1
ADS-B Aircraft Radar

Build a live map of every plane overhead — callsign, altitude, speed — pulled out of
the air onto your screen

Cost: ~$30
Difficulty:
Beginner-Intermediate
Build Time: 1 weekend
Why This Matters

Every airliner constantly broadcasts its identity, GPS position, altitude, and velocity in the clear on 1090
MHz — a system called ADS-B that is replacing radar for air-traffic control worldwide. There is no
encryption and no subscription: with a $30 software-defined radio and a small antenna, you can
receive those broadcasts directly and plot every aircraft in range on a live map, exactly like the
professional flight-tracking sites (which are largely built from volunteer receivers just like the one you
will build). It is the perfect first SDR project — the signal is strong, always present, and the payoff is
immediate and genuinely impressive: a real-time radar picture of the sky above you, decoded by
hardware you assembled.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand SDR fundamentals, pulse-position-modulated
digital signals (Mode S), antenna selection for a specific band, and real-time packet decoding.
Receiving and decoding a live aviation datalink is a concrete, demonstrable RF skill that maps
straight onto avionics, surveillance, and wireless-systems work.

→ The job this maps to: air-traffic / surveillance systems, avionics, and SDR/RF engineering —
flight-tracking networks, air-navigation service providers, and aerospace firms.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Eavesdrop on the Sky   •   Page 3
How It Works

• ADS-B on 1090 MHz: Aircraft transponders broadcast 'extended squitter' messages roughly twice a
second containing the 24-bit ICAO address, GPS latitude/longitude, altitude, speed, and callsign.
The signals are unencrypted and standardised worldwide, so any compatible receiver can decode
them.

• Pulse-position modulation: Mode S encodes bits as the position of short pulses within each
microsecond — a 1 Mbit/s pulse-position-modulated stream. The decoder samples fast enough to
distinguish pulse timing, reconstruct the message bits, and check them with a CRC.

• Antenna tuned to 1090 MHz: At 1090 MHz a quarter-wave is only ~6.9 cm, so a small ground-plane
or 'spider' antenna works and a collinear gives more range. Antenna length and placement (high,
clear of obstructions) matter far more than fancy electronics on this band.

• LNA and filter help range: Distant aircraft are weak and the band sits near strong cellular and pager
interference. A 1090 MHz SAW filter plus a low-noise amplifier at the antenna dramatically extends
range — from tens to a couple hundred kilometres line-of-sight.

• Decode and map (dump1090): Software like dump1090 demodulates the Mode S stream, validates
each message by CRC, and converts the position fields into latitude/longitude. It serves a live
browser map showing every aircraft's callsign, altitude, heading, and trail — a real-time radar
display you built.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Eavesdrop on the Sky   •   Page 4
Key Design Decisions
→ Why does ADS-B need no decryption? ADS-B was designed as an open air-traffic-control

broadcast so any aircraft or ground station can see the picture. Privacy of the broadcast was
deliberately traded for universal situational awareness — which is exactly why a hobbyist can
receive it legally.
→ Why is antenna height the biggest factor? 1090 MHz is line-of-sight; the radio horizon, not

transmit power, sets your range. Raising the antenna a few metres and clearing obstructions adds
far more range than any amplifier, because you are literally seeing farther over the curve of the
Earth.
→ Why a filter before the amplifier? Strong nearby signals (cellular, pagers) can overload a

broadband LNA and desensitise it. A SAW filter centred on 1090 MHz ahead of the LNA rejects
those, so the amplifier's gain goes to the signal you want instead of amplifying interference.

Build Steps

Plug in and scan: Install the RTL-SDR drivers and a general SDR app. Tune to 1090 MHz and
confirm you see brief bursts of activity — those are aircraft squitters. This proves the dongle and
antenna work before you add anything.

Build a 1090 MHz antenna: Make a quarter-wave ground-plane (a 6.9 cm vertical with four radials) or
a coaxial collinear for more gain. Mount it as high and clear as possible — a window or rooftop.
Connect with low-loss coax.

Add the LNA + filter: For more range, fit a 1090 MHz SAW-filtered LNA at the antenna and power it
via the dongle's bias-tee. Verify it is the 1090 MHz part — a wrong-band LNA will reduce performance.

Run dump1090: Install dump1090 (or readsb) on a Raspberry Pi or laptop, start it, and open the web
interface. Decoded aircraft appear with ICAO address, callsign, altitude, and speed.

PROJECT 2
TPMS Car-ID Sniffer

Reveal that every car driving past silently broadcasts a unique ID — it is not your
phone tracking you, it is your tires

Cost: ~$30
Difficulty: Intermediate
Build Time: 1 weekend
Why This Matters

Every modern car has tire-pressure sensors that periodically transmit on 315 MHz (North America) or
433 MHz (Europe) — and each transmission includes a unique sensor ID along with pressure and
temperature. They are unencrypted and broadcast whenever the wheels turn, which means a cheap
radio can log them. Researchers have shown TPMS IDs can be used to identify and track vehicles, and
this project lets you see that privacy gap with your own eyes: park near a road, decode the packets,
and watch unique IDs roll past. It is a striking lesson in how much our everyday devices leak — and
exactly the kind of wireless-security insight that automotive and IoT-security teams hire for.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand sub-GHz ISM transmission, OOK/FSK
demodulation, reverse-engineering an undocumented packet format, and the privacy implications of
unencrypted wireless — the core skill set of automotive RF and wireless-security engineering.

→ The job this maps to: automotive RF, wireless security / penetration testing, and
embedded-systems roles — automakers, Tier-1 suppliers, and IoT-security firms.

Legal & ethics: This is a receive-only demonstration of how much your own car leaks — best done
logging your own vehicles. Building a system to track other people by their TPMS IDs is a privacy
violation (and in many places regulated). Observe to understand the problem; do not operate it as a
surveillance tool.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Eavesdrop on the Sky   •   Page 7
How It Works

• TPMS transmissions: Each sensor wakes periodically (or on rotation) and transmits a short burst
with its unique 28-32 bit ID, the tire pressure, temperature, and a checksum. The bursts are
unencrypted and repeat every few seconds to a minute.

• 315 vs 433 MHz: North American cars typically use 315 MHz; European and many other markets use
433.92 MHz ISM. You tune the SDR to the right band for your region — the RTL-SDR covers both
easily.

• OOK and FSK modulation: TPMS sensors use on-off keying or frequency-shift keying with
Manchester or differential encoding. The decoder demodulates the chosen scheme, recovers the
bitstream, then aligns to the packet's preamble and sync word.

• Reverse-engineering the format: Different manufacturers pack the fields differently. Tools like
rtl_433 already know dozens of TPMS protocols; decoding a new one means finding the preamble,
the ID field, and how pressure and temperature are scaled — real protocol reverse-engineering.

• Seeing the privacy gap: Because the ID is static and unencrypted, the same car produces the same
ID every time it passes. Logging these is exactly how researchers demonstrated vehicle tracking —
and seeing your own car's IDs appear makes the abstract risk concrete.

Build Steps

Identify your band: Find whether your region/car uses 315 MHz or 433 MHz, tune the RTL-SDR
there, and look for short periodic bursts when a car is nearby or you roll your own.

Set up rtl_433: Install rtl_433, the open-source decoder that already understands many TPMS
protocols. Run it on your band; as cars pass or your own car rolls, decoded packets with IDs,
pressures, and temperatures print.

Confirm with your own car: Roll your own vehicle and watch its four sensor IDs appear, each with a
plausible pressure reading. Let a little air out of one tire and watch that sensor's value drop — proof
you are decoding real telemetry.

Log passing traffic (ethically): Park near a road and log the stream for a few minutes. Note how each
car contributes a cluster of repeating IDs — the dataset that demonstrates the tracking risk. Keep it to
understanding the problem, not profiling people.

Reverse a new protocol (bonus): If you hit a sensor rtl_433 does not recognise, capture the raw
burst, find the preamble and sync, and work out the ID and pressure fields. Decoding an unknown
format from scratch is a strong write-up.

→ What are the privacy implications of static, unencrypted device identifiers?
→ How could a manufacturer redesign TPMS to prevent tracking while keeping it cheap?

PROJECT 3
Radio Meteor Detector

Catch a ping for every shooting star as it ionizes the upper atmosphere — even in
daylight or solid cloud

Cost: ~$30
Difficulty: Intermediate
Build Time: 1 weekend
Why This Matters

When a meteor streaks through the upper atmosphere it leaves a trail of ionized gas that briefly reflects
radio waves — and you can hear it. By tuning to a powerful distant VHF transmitter that is normally
below your horizon (a dedicated radar like GRAVES, or a far-off TV or FM carrier), you receive
nothing... until a meteor trail bounces that signal over the horizon to your antenna, producing a sudden
'ping.' This is forward-scatter meteor detection, and it works day or night, through clouds, even when
you cannot see a thing. You are detecting objects from space by their effect on radio propagation —
real radio-astronomy technique, built from a $30 dongle and a simple antenna.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand weak-signal reception, the radio horizon and
forward-scatter propagation, narrowband detection and spectrograms, and distinguishing real events
from noise. It is a genuine radio-astronomy instrumentation skill that maps onto research, defence,
and DSP roles.

→ The job this maps to: radio-astronomy instrumentation, weak-signal RF, and DSP roles —
research institutions, observatories, and signal-processing teams.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Eavesdrop on the Sky   •   Page 11
How It Works

• Forward-scatter geometry: You point a directional antenna toward a powerful VHF transmitter
hundreds to ~1500 km away — far enough that it is below your horizon and you normally receive
nothing on its frequency. The transmitter and you form a 'bistatic' pair waiting for something to
bounce the signal across.

• Meteors make a mirror: A meteoroid hitting the atmosphere at tens of km/s ionizes a column of air
~80-120 km up. That plasma trail briefly reflects VHF radio: for a fraction of a second to a few
seconds, the distant transmitter's carrier is scattered down to your antenna — a 'ping.'

• Choosing the transmitter: Dedicated beacons like the French GRAVES radar (143.05 MHz) are
ideal where receivable; elsewhere, distant analog TV or FM carriers, or amateur beacons, serve the
same role. You tune precisely to the carrier and look for reflections, not the direct signal.

• Detecting the ping: Software (SDR# plus a spectrogram, or a dedicated detector) shows a waterfall
of the narrow frequency around the carrier. A meteor appears as a sudden bright trace — often
Doppler-shifted as the trail drifts — lasting from a fraction of a second to many seconds for a bright
fireball.

• Counting and timing: Logging pings over hours reveals meteor activity, including the dramatic rise
during showers like the Perseids. Because radio does not care about daylight or clouds, you detect
meteors a visual observer never could — including the daytime showers.

Build Steps

Pick a transmitter + frequency: Choose a powerful VHF source beyond your horizon — GRAVES at
143.05 MHz if you are in range, otherwise a distant TV/FM carrier or beacon. Note its exact frequency
and compass bearing from you.

Aim a Yagi at it: Build or buy a small VHF Yagi for that frequency and point it toward the transmitter's
bearing, tilted up slightly toward the reflection region. Directionality rejects local noise and favours the
scatter path.

Tune precisely to the carrier: In your SDR software, tune exactly to the transmitter frequency with a
narrow bandwidth. With no meteor you should see only noise (the direct signal is over the horizon).
This 'silent' baseline is what makes pings obvious.

Watch the waterfall: Open a spectrogram zoomed tight on the carrier. When a meteor passes, a
bright streak appears — sometimes a sharp dot, sometimes a long Doppler-curved trace for a bright
event. Confirm a few by ear (a sudden whistle or ping).

Log and correlate: Run an automatic detector or log manually over a night, counting pings per hour.
Compare a normal night to a meteor-shower peak and plot the rate — your own radio meteor-activity
curve.
Interview Questions:
→ What physically reflects the radio signal during a meteor detection?
→ Why must the reference transmitter be beyond your horizon for forward scatter to work?
→ Why can radio detect meteors in daylight and through clouds when optical cannot?
→ What causes the Doppler shift seen on a meteor ping?
→ How do you distinguish a genuine meteor ping from aircraft reflections or interference?
→ How would you automate counting and characterising pings over a long observation?

PROJECT 4
AIS Ship Tracker

The maritime cousin of ADS-B — live positions, names, headings, and cargo of every
ship in range

Cost: ~$35
Difficulty:
Beginner-Intermediate
Build Time: 1 weekend
Why This Matters

Ships continuously broadcast their identity, GPS position, course, speed, and cargo type on marine
VHF (161.975 and 162.025 MHz) using a system called AIS — the maritime equivalent of aircraft
ADS-B. It is unencrypted and required on most large vessels, so with an SDR tuned to the marine band
you can plot live ship traffic on a map: tankers, ferries, fishing boats, naval auxiliaries, each with its
name and destination. If you are anywhere near a coast, port, or large river, the result is a busy
real-time picture of maritime traffic — and the same volunteer-receiver model behind the public
ship-tracking sites.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand VHF reception, GMSK demodulation, the
AIS/NMEA message format, and multi-channel decoding. Receiving and plotting a live maritime
datalink is a concrete RF and decoding skill directly relevant to maritime, surveillance, and
wireless-systems work.

→ The job this maps to: maritime / navigation systems, coastal surveillance, and SDR/RF roles —
shipping, port authorities, defence, and tracking networks.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Eavesdrop on the Sky   •   Page 14
How It Works

• AIS on marine VHF: The Automatic Identification System broadcasts on two channels near 162
MHz. Vessels send their MMSI identity, GPS position, course, speed, and (in static messages) ship
name, type, and destination, on a self-organising time-division schedule so many ships share the
channel.

• Two channels at once: AIS uses 161.975 MHz (channel A) and 162.025 MHz (channel B). A
capable receiver decodes both simultaneously — the RTL-SDR's bandwidth easily spans both, and
the decoder splits and demodulates each.

• GMSK modulation: AIS uses Gaussian minimum-shift keying at 9600 bps — a compact,
constant-envelope FSK variant. The decoder demodulates GMSK, recovers the HDLC-framed
packets, and checks each with a CRC.

• NMEA decoding: Valid packets are turned into NMEA AIS sentences (the same format chartplotters
use). Software like AIS-catcher or rtl-ais parses these into position and vessel-info records.

• Plot the traffic: Feed the decoded positions to a map (AIS-catcher's web UI or a plotter). Ships
appear with names, headings, and tracks; static messages fill in type and destination. Near a coast
you will see a constantly updating maritime picture.

PROJECT 5
433 MHz Sensor Decoder

Decode the invisible chatter of the ISM band — weather stations, doorbells,
thermometers, your own smart-home sensors

Cost: ~$25
Difficulty:
Beginner-Intermediate
Build Time: 1 weekend
Why This Matters

The 433 MHz ISM band is full of chatter you never notice: wireless weather stations, remote
thermometers, soil-moisture sensors, doorbells, garage remotes, and cheap smart-home gadgets all
transmit there in the clear. Point an SDR at it and an open-source decoder turns that noise into
readable data — temperatures, humidity, button presses, sensor IDs — from devices all around your
neighbourhood and inside your own home. It is the most approachable possible introduction to IoT
reverse-engineering, and the natural gateway to building your own sensor network or auditing what
your devices leak. The same skills underpin IoT product development and wireless security.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand sub-GHz ISM communication, OOK/FSK
demodulation, packet framing and checksums, and decoding undocumented device protocols. This
is exactly the wireless skill set behind IoT product engineering and connected-device security.

→ The job this maps to: IoT / embedded wireless, home-automation, and wireless-security roles —
IoT product companies, smart-home platforms, and security teams.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Eavesdrop on the Sky   •   Page 17
How It Works

• The 433 MHz ISM band: 433.92 MHz is a licence-free band where countless low-power devices
transmit short, simple messages. Because the band is shared and cheap, manufacturers use
unencrypted OOK/FSK with basic framing — easy to receive and decode.

• OOK and FSK: Most cheap sensors use on-off keying (the carrier blips on and off) or simple FSK.
The decoder demodulates the carrier into a raw pulse train, then interprets pulse widths as bits
using each protocol's encoding (PWM, Manchester, and so on).

• Packet framing and IDs: A typical message has a preamble, a device ID, the payload (temperature,
humidity, state), and a checksum. The ID lets you tell your neighbour's weather station from your
own; the checksum lets the decoder reject corrupted packets.

• rtl_433 does the heavy lifting: rtl_433 is an open-source decoder that recognises hundreds of
device protocols out of the box. Run it and it auto-identifies known devices, printing manufacturer,
model, ID, and decoded values as JSON you can log or pipe anywhere.

• Decode the unknown: When you hit a device rtl_433 does not know, you capture the raw signal,
study the pulse pattern, and work out the encoding and fields yourself — a clean, self-contained
protocol reverse-engineering project that is genuinely impressive on a resume.

PROJECT 6
Radiosonde Tracker & Recovery

Lock onto a weather balloon's telemetry as it falls from 30 km up — then go physically
chase it down

Cost: ~$35
Difficulty: Intermediate
Build Time: 1-2 weekends
Why This Matters

Twice a day, from hundreds of sites worldwide, weather agencies launch balloons carrying
radiosondes — small instrument packages that transmit temperature, humidity, pressure, and GPS
position as they rise to ~30 km, then parachute back to Earth. Those transmissions (around 400-406
MHz) are unencrypted, so you can receive a sonde's live telemetry, plot its track, and — using its GPS
position and a descent model — predict where it will land and go recover it. It is a genuine treasure
hunt powered by RF: decode a real aerospace telemetry stream, do the tracking and prediction math,
and end up holding the instrument you tracked from the edge of space. Recovered sondes are also
reusable for your own high-altitude projects.

What this proves to a recruiter: You understand telemetry decoding, GNSS position data,
weak-signal VHF/UHF reception with directional antennas, and trajectory prediction. Tracking a live
aerospace telemetry payload from launch to landing is a standout, end-to-end RF-and-data skill for
aerospace and telemetry roles.

→ The job this maps to: telemetry / GNSS, aerospace / avionics, and RF-systems roles — weather
agencies, aerospace firms, and high-altitude ballooning teams.

Recovery etiquette: Recovering a landed radiosonde is legal in most places (they are considered
abandoned), but the chase is the risky part: do not trespass, do not enter roads or rail, and respect
private property and local rules. Use the telemetry to predict the landing site, then knock and ask
before crossing anyone's land.
@1nska   •   6 EE Projects That Eavesdrop on the Sky   •   Page 20
How It Works

• Radiosonde telemetry: A radiosonde (commonly a Vaisala RS41 or Graw type) transmits a
continuous data frame with its GPS latitude, longitude, and altitude plus temperature, humidity, and
pressure, on a frequency in the 400-406 MHz meteorological band. Each launch site uses a known
frequency you can look up.

• Receiving the signal: As the balloon climbs it becomes line-of-sight over a huge area, so reception
is easy at altitude; the hard part is the low-altitude descent and landing. A directional UHF antenna
(a small Yagi) and an LNA help you hold the signal as the sonde drops behind terrain.

• Decoding the frame: Software like radiosonde_auto_rx demodulates the sonde's FSK telemetry,
decodes the frame format for that sonde type, validates it, and outputs live position and sensor data
— often uploading to a tracking map automatically.

• Predicting the landing: Once you have the descent trajectory and the sonde's current position and
altitude, a descent model (accounting for wind drift under the parachute) predicts the landing spot.
The prediction tightens as the sonde nears the ground.

• The recovery: With a predicted landing zone, you drive toward it, switch to a handheld Yagi for the
final direction-finding, and home in on the last-known position. Recovering the payload is the
tangible payoff — and the sonde can be reflashed for your own balloon or tracking experiments.

Build Steps

Find a launch + frequency: Look up your nearest radiosonde launch site, its schedule (often ~00:00
and 12:00 UTC), and the transmit frequency. Sites and live sondes are listed on public tracking maps.

Set up auto_rx: Install radiosonde_auto_rx on a Raspberry Pi or laptop with the RTL-SDR. Configure
your frequency range; it will scan, detect a sonde, lock on, and decode its telemetry automatically.

Track the flight: Once decoding, watch the sonde's live position, altitude, and sensor data. Follow it up
to burst altitude (~30 km) and into descent. auto_rx can upload to a map so you see the whole
trajectory.

Predict the landing: Use the descent prediction (built into the tracking tools) to estimate the landing
zone from current position, altitude, and wind. Refine as it drops — the cone narrows quickly near the
ground.

Drive out and recover: Head toward the predicted site, switch to a handheld Yagi to direction-find the
final signal, and locate the payload. Respect property and access rules. Reflash the recovered sonde
for your own projects if you like.

The sky is full of signals nobody's listening to.
One $30 radio, and you are.

Aircraft, ships, weather balloons, meteors, and the sensors all around you are broadcasting constantly,
in the clear, to anyone with a receiver. With a single software-defined radio and the right antenna, you
can pull all of it out of the air and decode it yourself — a live radar of the sky, a map of the seas, a ping
for every shooting star. The hardware is cheap; the skill is in the antennas, the weak-signal reception,
and the protocol decoding.

And here is the throughline that makes it more than a hobby: every one of these is receive-only and
legal, and that restraint is exactly what real RF and security engineers practise. Decoding what is
already public, understanding what leaks, and respecting what is private is the professional version of
this craft. SDR, aerospace surveillance, maritime systems, and signals work all hire people who can do
precisely this.

Build even one of these. Screenshot the live map, log the data, plot your range. Put it on your GitHub
with a proper README and a note on the legal, receive-only scope. You will have a portfolio piece
that proves you can pull real signals out of the air — and the judgment to do it responsibly.
